title: Firewalls, IDS and intruders
syllabusUnit: Unit V: Firewalls, Intrusion Detection & Intruders
covers: Packet filters, stateful inspection, IDS/IPS, intruders, honeypots
learningGoals: You will be able to construct packet filtering and stateful inspection firewall rules.
You will be able to distinguish an Intrusion Detection System (IDS) from an Intrusion Prevention System (IPS).
You will be able to explain how Honeypots lure and analyze attackers.

lessonCards.title: The Network Bouncer: Firewalls
lessonCards.analogy: A security guard at a building lobby checking badges against a strict entry list.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Packet Filtering firewalls inspect IP addresses and port numbers in isolation. Stateful Inspection tracks live TCP connection states (SYN, ESTABLISHED), blocking unsolicited packets.
lessonCards.example: Default policy: Deny All incoming traffic; allow only established outbound replies.

lessonCards.title: Watchtowers: IDS vs IPS
lessonCards.analogy: An alarm bell ringing when a burglar climbs the fence (IDS) vs an automated gate that slams shut (IPS).
lessonCards.coreConcept: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) monitors traffic for known attack signatures or anomalies and raises alerts. An Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) sits inline and drops malicious packets in real time.
lessonCards.example: Signature-based detection spots known exploits (Snort rules); anomaly-based detection spots unusual traffic spikes.

lessonCards.title: Honeypots: The Decoy Vault
lessonCards.analogy: A fake bank safe filled with marked monopoly money and hidden motion-detector cameras.
lessonCards.coreConcept: A honeypot is an intentionally vulnerable decoy server designed to lure attackers, detect zero-day techniques, and waste adversary resources without exposing real assets.
lessonCards.example: Honeynets provide early threat intelligence on automated scanner botnets.

questions.prompt: What is the key advantage of a 'Stateful Inspection' firewall over a stateless packet filter?
options: Stateful firewalls track TCP connection states, automatically allowing response packets for established outbound connections
Stateful firewalls never need rules
Stateful firewalls run on batteries
Stateful firewalls decrypt all RSA keys
questions.explanation: A stateful firewall knows when an internal client initiated an outbound request, allowing inbound response packets on dynamic ports without leaving ports permanently open.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Stateful inspection maintains a dynamic state table of active sessions.
Firewalls require explicit security rule configurations.
Power source is unrelated to packet inspection logic.
Firewalls do not crack RSA keys.
questions.realWorldExample: Linux iptables/nftables and Cisco ASA firewalls operate stateful connection tracking engines.

questions.prompt: What is the critical operational difference between an Intrusion Detection System (IDS) and an Intrusion Prevention System (IPS)?
options: An IDS passively alerts on suspicious traffic; an IPS sits inline and actively drops malicious packets
An IDS only runs on Linux; an IPS runs on Mac
An IDS is hardware; an IPS is a word document
An IPS cannot inspect packets
questions.explanation: An IDS receives a mirrored copy of network packets (SPAN port) and generates alerts. An IPS sits directly inline in the packet flow to actively block attacks.
wrongExplanations: Correct! IDS alerts defenders; IPS blocks threats in real time.
Both systems deploy across Linux, BSD, and proprietary network appliances.
Both are advanced network security systems.
Both perform deep packet inspection.
questions.realWorldExample: Snort and Suricata can run in either passive IDS mode or active inline IPS mode.

questions.prompt: What is a 'DMZ' (Demilitarized Zone) in network security architecture?
options: A screened perimeter subnet hosting public-facing servers (web, mail) isolated from the internal corporate network
A zone where security rules are disabled
A computer with no operating system
A private chatroom for hackers
questions.explanation: A DMZ places internet-accessible servers behind an external firewall so if a web server is compromised, attackers cannot directly pivot into internal databases.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Dual-firewall DMZ architectures segment public services from internal LAN assets.
Security rules are strictly enforced in DMZs.
DMZ hosts run hardened operating systems.
DMZ is an enterprise network architecture.
questions.realWorldExample: Standard enterprise designs place web servers in the DMZ and database servers in the protected internal tier.

questions.prompt: What is the primary function of a 'Honeypot' in a defensive security operations center?
options: To act as an attractive decoy system that traps attackers and gathers intelligence on exploit methods
To store company honey inventory
To encrypt user passwords
To speed up internet connectivity
questions.explanation: Honeypots have no legitimate production value; any interaction with a honeypot is by definition suspicious or malicious, providing clean threat telemetry.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Decoys detect automated scanners, zero-days, and lateral movement.
Agricultural tracking is unrelated.
Honeypots do not handle authentication.
Honeypots do not route user traffic.
questions.realWorldExample: Canary tokens and Cowrie SSH honeypots alert defenders the moment an intruder probes an internal network.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended 'Default Firewall Stance' for securing high-risk network interfaces?
options: Default Deny: drop all traffic unless explicitly permitted by an authorized rule
Default Allow: permit all traffic and block only known bad websites
Allow all traffic on weekends
Randomly drop 50% of all packets
questions.explanation: A Default Deny (whitelist) stance ensures that new ports or unapproved protocols are automatically blocked unless an administrator explicitly opens them.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Whitelisting minimizes attack surface by blocking all unauthorized ingress.
Default Allow exposes all services to scanning and zero-day attacks.
Calendar-based policies leave systems vulnerable on weekends.
Random dropping destroys network reliability.
questions.realWorldExample: PCI-DSS and ISO 27001 mandate Default Deny policies on all corporate network boundaries.

questions.prompt: How does an 'Anomaly-Based' Intrusion Detection System detect potential zero-day attacks?
options: It establishes a statistical baseline of normal network behavior and flags significant deviations
It searches for exact matching antivirus signatures
It asks the user if they are a hacker
It scans for misspelled words in emails
questions.explanation: Because zero-day attacks have no existing signatures, anomaly detection spots abnormal traffic volume, unusual port combinations, or foreign protocols.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Baseline deviations allow detecting novel attacks before signatures exist.
Signature matching only spots previously documented exploits.
Attackers do not self-identify.
Spelling checks are text processing.
questions.realWorldExample: Modern SIEM and XDR platforms use machine learning models for anomaly detection on network telemetry.

ashRecap: Firewalls are your castle gates; default to 'Deny All'! IDS and IPS watch the perimeter day and night to spot intruders before they breach the keep!
